frameworks.name: Scaling Through Training vs Selection
frameworks.definition: Two paths to grow a sales organization: scaling through selection (hire many, let weak performers exit) vs. scaling through training (teach anyone off the street to sell at high performance). Scaling through training yields superior margins and competitive advantage.

frameworks.name: Profit-Driver Identification in Scaling
frameworks.definition: In a scaling coaching business, the two most profitable customer segments are those acquired for free (organic) and those who renew without paying CAC again. All paid-acquisition customers in the middle serve primarily to unlock scale. Focus compounds on these two drivers.

claims.text: In coaching/info product businesses, a 2:1 LTV:CAC ratio (as this business had) creates insufficient margin cushion to scale a growing sales team without approaching unprofitability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Coaching or info product business model
Paid acquisition channel at 70% of revenue
Sales team growing rapidly (4→40 reps in 3 months)
bounded_by: Does not apply to high-margin SaaS (different unit economics)
Does not apply to businesses with strong organic channel dominance

claims.text: When a paid-acquisition coaching business runs at 2:1 LTV:CAC and the organic channel (free traffic) carries 20% of margins while paid carries 80%, removing the organic channel would render the business unprofitable despite high sales volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Coaching/info model with 70% paid, 30% organic mix
Organic customers at higher-than-average unit margin
claims.mechanism: Organic customers have zero CAC, so they absorb overhead and contribute full margin; paid customers at 2:1 LTV:CAC consume the margin gains and create scaling friction.

claims.text: In a rapidly-scaled sales team (4→40 reps in 3 months), new rep ramp depresses overall close rate because the average is pulled down by immature reps still in onboarding. Median close rate of mature reps (30-35%) exceeds team average (20%) by 50-75%.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-velocity sales team scaling (quad 10x growth in headcount)
Complex sales close requiring weeks of ramp

anchors.region: current team average (inflated new rep cohort)

claims.text: The primary path to increasing LTV (and thus improving CAC:LTV ratio) in a service business is improving sales team close rate through better recruitment and training, not creative optimization or front-end conversion rate improvements.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business model with consultative close
Current close rate at 20%, team average vs. 30-35% potential
Sales team scaled rapidly without corresponding training investment
claims.mechanism: Better-trained reps close higher percentage of leads, converting same lead volume into higher revenue per lead (increasing dollars-per-lead, thus LTV).
bounded_by: Does not apply if close rate is already 40%+ (approaching market ceiling)
Does not apply if the bottleneck is lead quality rather than sales execution

claims.text: Scaling a sales organization through training (teaching any new hire to perform) yields higher margins and competitive advantage compared to scaling through selection (hiring mercenaries and filtering out poor performers), because trained sellers command lower pay, ramp faster, and have lower turnover.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sales-driven business model
High-touch consultative close
Ability to document and systematize sales process
claims.mechanism: Training converts commodity labor into differentiated sellers; untrained mercenaries demand premium pay and leave when offered slightly higher compensation elsewhere. Trained sellers have lower alternative value and stay, reducing replacement cost and payroll burden.
bounded_by: Does not apply to 1-click commoditized sales (low-ticket transactional)
Does not apply if the sales process is inherently non-teachable (pure relationship/charisma-based)

claims.text: When a service business targets $100M revenue from $33M at 2:1 LTV:CAC, the 80-20 priority is improving the sales function (close rate, team quality, training) to achieve 4:1 to 5:1 LTV:CAC, which unlocks the scale required for profitability at that revenue tier.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Revenue goal: $33M → $100M (3x scale)
Current LTV:CAC: 2:1 (insufficient margin)
Current close rate: 20% (below mature rep baseline)
claims.mechanism: Improving close rate from 20% to 30-35% (via better reps) increases revenue-per-lead 50-75%, directly improving LTV and unlocking margin for sales team growth.
bounded_by: Assumes paid-acquisition channel remains viable at scale (media arbitrage possible)
Does not apply if organic channel collapses or ads stop performing

claims.text: In a scaling coaching business, the two customer acquisition sources contributing most to profit (organic customers with zero CAC and customers renewing without additional CAC) should be actively doubled down on, while paid-acquisition customers are treated as supporting infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Coaching or info-product model with mixed acquisition (paid + organic)
Renewable customer base (subscription or annual renewal)
bounded_by: Does not apply if business is one-time transaction (no renewal path)
Does not apply if organic channel is negligible (< 10% of revenue)

claims.text: Doubling sales team size (40 → 80 reps) at a 2:1 LTV:CAC ratio is operationally infeasible without first improving close rate to 30-35% and achieving 4:1 LTV:CAC, because each new rep added at low close rate increases burn without corresponding revenue increase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Current close rate below 25%
Current LTV:CAC below 3:1
Sales team payroll growing faster than revenue
claims.mechanism: New rep at 20% close rate generates lower revenue-per-rep than payroll + CAC spend; unit economics are negative until close rate improves, so hiring more reps before fixing close rate compounds the problem.

examples.text: In this business, scaling from 4 sales reps to 40 in 3 months created a cohort with wide performance variance. The top reps close at ~40%, but the team average is 20% because so many reps are still in ramp. Once the new cohort matures, the median should approach the mature-rep baseline of 30-35%, raising overall team efficiency without additional hiring.

The business had 70% of customers from paid acquisition and 30% from organic (free). Despite organic representing only 30% of customers, it contributes 20% of total margins because these customers have zero CAC. Paid customers contribute 80% of margins despite being 70% of volume, meaning each paid customer is lower-margin than each organic customer. Removing the organic channel would render the business unprofitable.

The founder personally developed the sales training and playbook, which was refined over time based on top-rep performance. This bespoke training is now the asset differentiating the business from competitors who hire mercenary salespeople. The challenge is scaling the training to raise the median rep from 20% close to 30-35%, allowing the business to hire more reps without margin compression.

practices.text: When identifying the primary constraint in a scaling business, separate surface-level symptoms (high sales volume, low margins) from root causes (weak reps, poor training, weak close rate). The operating expense budget and hiring plan should target root cause, not symptom.

For coaching or info-product businesses at 2:1 LTV:CAC, focus on improving close rate through better sales team recruitment and training before investing in sales-team expansion. Each ramp from 20% to 30-35% close rate adds 50% revenue-per-lead without increasing media spend.

Document and systematize the sales close process, onboarding, and playbook such that new hires off the street can reach median performance (30-35% close rate) within 4-8 weeks. This scaling-through-training approach yields 3-5x higher margins than scaling-through-selection (hiring proven mercenaries).
